'''''Pseudopodospermum hispanicum''''', commonly known as '''black salsify''' or '''Spanish salsify''', also known as '''black oyster plant''', '''serpent root''', '''viper's herb''', '''viper's grass''' or '''scorzonera''', is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] species of plant in the sunflower family ([[Asteraceae]]), cultivated as a [[root vegetable]] in the same way as purple salsify (''[[Tragopogon porrifolius]]''), also in the sunflower family.<ref name="Wild Flowers Worth Knowing">{{cite book |last1=Blanchan |first1=Neltje |title=Wild Flowers Worth Knowing |date=2005 |publisher=Project Gutenberg Literary Archive Foundation}}</ref> It is native to Southern Europe and cultivated as a crop in [[Southern Europe|Southern]] and [[Central Europe]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Granica|first=Sebastian|date=2015|title=Qualitative and quantitative analyses of secondary metabolites in aerial and subaerial of Scorzonera hispanica L. (black salsify|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0308814614015635 |journal=Food Chemistry|volume=173|pages=321–331|doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2014.10.006 |pmid=25466029 |url-access=subscription}}</ref> It grows on nutrient poor soils, dry [[pasture]], rocky areas, in [[thicket]]s and on [[Lime (material)|limy]] or [[marl]]y soils of [[Temperate climate|temperate zones]].<ref name="Bermejo, Neglected Crops" />

==Description==
[[File:Scorzonera hispanica 001.JPG|thumb|right|Flowering ''Pseudopodospermum hispanicum'']]
''Pseudopodospermum hispanicum'' is grown commercially as an [[annual plant|annual]], although it is a [[biennial plant]]. After a vegetative phase in the first year, the plant flowers in its second year and can reach a height of 60 cm with a stem diameter of 5 cm. The [[Hermaphroditic (botany)|hermaphroditic]] flowers are insect-pollinated.<ref name="rana_vcs">{{cite book|last1=Rana|first1=M.K.|title=Vegetable Crop Science|date=2017|publisher=CRC Press|edition=1st}}</ref> The flower-head is terminal and consists of yellow ray [[florets]]. The stem is smooth and leafy and the leaves are [[lanceolate]] to [[Ovate (botany)|ovate]] with entire margins.<ref name="Bastgen, C.; Schröder, B.; Zurlutter, S. (2017). “Welche essbare Wildpflanze ist das?” Kosmos (in German): 108">{{cite book |last1=Bastgen |first1=Christa |last2=Schröder |first2=Berko |last3=Zurlutter |first3=Stefanie |title=Welche essbare Wildpflanze ist das? |date=2017 |publisher=Franckh-Kosmos Verlags-GmbH & Co.KG |location=Stuttgart |isbn=978-3-440-15193-8 |page=108 |edition=1}}</ref> Black salsify forms a long cylindrical [[taproot]] with a brownish to black cork layer. If harvested young, the carrot-like roots are tender, long and tapered with shiny white flesh.<ref name="rana_vcs" /> They contain a milky [[latex]], which turns the roots black when exposed to air.<ref name="Bastgen, C.; Schröder, B.; Zurlutter, S. (2017). “Welche essbare Wildpflanze ist das?” Kosmos (in German): 108" />

==History==  
Black salsify is native to Southern Europe and the [[Near East]].<ref name="Bermejo, Neglected Crops" /> As is indicated by its [[binomial name]], it is generally thought to have spread to the rest of Europe from Spain, but the first mention of the vegetable by a Western writer came from [[Leonhard Rauwolf]], who reported seeing scorzonera at the market of [[Aleppo]] in Syria, in 1575. In 1612, François Gentil, in his ''Le Jardinier Solitaire'' (The Lonely Gardener), described the Spanish salsify as the best root which can be grown in gardens.<ref name="Sturtevant1890">{{cite journal |last=Sturtevant |first=E.L. |author-link=Edward Lewis Sturtevant |title=History of Garden Vegetables (Continued)|journal=The American Naturalist |volume=24 |issue=283 |page=643 |date=1890 |jstor=2450936 }}</ref> By 1683, the use of the root as a garden vegetable is recorded in England.<ref name="Sturtevant1890"/> Quintyne in France, in 1690, calls it "one of our chiefest roots."<ref name="Sturtevant1890"/> 

It was believed that the plant makes a good antidote against bites of venomous animals.<ref name="Bermejo, Neglected Crops" />{{rp|323}} Based on this, it was often claimed that the name scorzonera derives from the [[Old French]] word ''scorzon'' meaning snake (or "adder" to be exact). The most likely etymological root, though, is the [[Catalan language|Catalan]] word ''escurçonera'', deriving from ''escurçó'' (viper), where the suffix -nera conveys an association or use with regards to vipers. ''Scorzonera'' must be an italian transliteration of ''escurçonera'', explained by the long Catalan presence in Sardinia and southern Italy, influencing local languages between the 14th and 18th centuries. Less likely, the name might derive from Italian ''scorza negra'' meaning "black bark"/"black peel", after the dark brown to black skin of the root. The plant was being cultivated as a vegetable in Italy and France by 1660 and, soon after,{{when|date=October 2019}} vast fields were grown of it in what is now Belgium.{{vague|date=October 2019}}<!-- Belgium became a nation state in 1830, "Belgian" as a nationality didn't exist until then -->

==Nutritional value==
Black salsify is considered [[nutritious]]: it contains [[protein]]s, [[fat]]s, [[asparagine]], [[choline]], laevulin, as well as minerals such as [[potassium]], [[calcium]], [[phosphorus]], [[iron]], [[sodium]], and [[vitamin]]s A, B<sub>1</sub>, E and C. It also contains the [[polysaccharide]] [[inulin]], conferring a mild sweetness that is suitable for [[diabetic]]s.<ref name="Bermejo, Neglected Crops" /> Inulin, used as a [[Dietary fiber|dietary fibre]], may have a positive effect on the [[Human digestive system|digestive system]], [[Circulatory system|blood circulation]], [[kidney]]s and inhibit cancerous processes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Hyun-Na|first=Koo|date=2003|title=Inulin stimulates NO synthesis via activation of PKC-􏰀 and protein tyrosine kinase, resulting in the activation of NF-􏰁B by IFN-􏰂-primed RAW 264.7 cells|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0955286303001311|journal=Journal of Nutritional Biochemistry|volume=14|issue=10 |pages=598–605|doi=10.1016/j.jnutbio.2003.07.002 |pmid=14559111 |via=Elsevier Science Direct|url-access=subscription}}</ref>
[[Image:Schwarzwurzeln.jpg|thumb|Black salsify roots]]

==Preparation==
Various parts of the plant can be consumed, including roots, leafy shoots, and open flowers, either cooked or raw.<ref name="rana_vcs" /> The principal product however are the stem tuber roots.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cappers|first1=R.T.J|last2=Neef|first2=R.|last3=Bekker|first3=R. M.|last4=Fantone|first4=F.|last5=Okur|first5=Y.|date=2016|title=Digital atlas of traditional agricultural practices and food processing|journal=Barkhuis Publishing & Groningen University Library|volume=Groningen archaeological studies; Vol. 301572|issue=1760}}</ref>
The thick black skin of the salsify root is usually considered inedible and can be removed either prior to or after [[boiling]]. If the skin is removed prior to boiling, the peeled root should be immediately immersed in water mixed with vinegar or lemon juice, in order to prevent discolouring. Since the root contains an extremely sticky [[latex]], it is often more convenient to peel it after boiling the root for 20 to 25 minutes (or less). Residue of the latex can be removed by rubbing with a drop of oil and then washing with soap.

Black salsify is often eaten together with other vegetables, such as [[pea]]s and [[carrot]]s. But it is also popular served like asparagus in a white [[sauce]], such as [[bechamel sauce]], [[Mustard (condiment)|mustard sauce]] or [[hollandaise sauce]]. Boiled salsify roots may also be coated with [[Batter (cooking)|batter]] and [[Deep frying|deep fried]].
The young roots are used in salads and the salsify latex can be used as [[chewing gum]].<ref name="rana_vcs" /> Flowering shoots are consumed similarly to [[asparagus]] and the flowers can be added to salads, together with brown seedlings or the long clumps of grass-like green leaves.<ref name="rana_vcs" />

The '''scorzonera sweet''' is a crystallized dessert made from scorzonera in [[Évora]], [[Alentejo]], Portugal. It is listed on the [[Ark of Taste]].<ref>[https://www.fondazioneslowfood.com/en/ark-of-taste-slow-food/scorzonera-sweet/ Scorzonera sweet] Slow Food Foundation</ref>

==Cultivation==

[[File:SchwarzwurzelBestandShispanica.jpg|thumb|Commercial production in Germany]]
Black salsify is hitherto mainly a European crop. Belgium, France and the Netherlands are the world's largest producers of black salsify; significant amounts are also produced in Germany.<ref name="Hortipendium" /><ref name="Bermejo, Neglected Crops" /> In the latter country, 'Hoffmanns Schwarzer Pfahl' is a [[cultivar]] widely used by commercial growers, while 'Duplex' is popular among small-scale gardeners.<ref name="Hortigate">{{cite web |last1=Postweiler |first1=Karin |last2=Regner |first2=Simon |title=Versuche im Deutschen Gartenbau 2019 |url=https://www.hortigate.de/bericht?nr=86504 |website=Hortigate |publisher=DLR Rheinpfalz |access-date=9 November 2021}}</ref> Some other cultivars are commercially available, but because it was a rather localized crop before being produced for a wider market there are comparatively few [[landrace]]s. Collections of local races and old cultivars can be found at the [[Nordic Genetic Resource Center]] in Sweden<ref name="NordGen">{{cite web |title=Nordic Genetic Resource Bank |url=https://www.nordgen.org/en/ |website=NordGen |access-date=9 November 2021}}</ref> and the [[Vavilov center|Vavilov]] Institute of Plant-Genetic Resources<ref name="Vavilov Institute">{{cite web |title=Vavilov All-Russian Institute of Plant Genetic Resources (VIR) |url=https://www.vir.nw.ru/en/ |website=vir.nw.ru |publisher=VIR |access-date=9 November 2021}}</ref> in Russia.<ref name="Bermejo, Neglected Crops" />

Breeding objectives are reduced susceptibility to [[Bolting (horticulture)|bolting]], low percentage of roots with cavities, improved suitability for mechanical sowing and harvesting, as well as for industrial processing.<ref name="Bermejo, Neglected Crops" />

=== Sowing ===
Scorzonera is sown in early spring, preferably at the end of April.<ref name = "Vulsteke">{{cite journal |last1=Vulsteke |first1=G. |title=Harvest-time in relation to sowing time of Scorzonera (Scorzonera hispanica L.) |journal=Acta Horticulturae |date=1979 |issue=93 |pages=101–112|doi=10.17660/ActaHortic.1979.93.12 }}</ref> Sowing too early can result in early flowering and loss of yield. About 12 kg of [[seed]]s per hectare are required. The seeds are sown directly into shallow [[furrows]] at a depth of 1.5 – 2 cm with 30–50 cm in between them. Plants should stand at a density of 50 plants/m<sup>2</sup> for optimal yield. Because of the seeds’ unusual shape, machine sowing is difficult. Storage of seeds is also a critical point, as [[germination]] is usually only guaranteed for 1–2 years. Optimal storage conditions are dry and cool.<ref name="Hortipendium" />

=== Soil requirements ===
The roots develop best in very light textured, sandy [[soil]]. Any stones or gravel in the ground can cause root deformation. Ideal [[pH]] values are between 5.8 – 6.5 and [[Liming (soil)|liming]] is recommended for more acidic soils. A high [[humus]] content is beneficial.<ref name="Hortipendium">{{cite web |title=Schwarzwurzel |url=https://www.hortipendium.de/Schwarzwurzel |website=Hortipendium |publisher=DLR Rheinpfalz |access-date=9 November 2021}}</ref> Generally, the species can grow in a variety of conditions and has potential to be grown as a [[cash crop]] in less favorable, marginal environments in [[Temperate climate|temperate]] zones.<ref name="Pereira et al.">{{cite journal |last1=Pereira |first1=I.P. |last2=Dias |first2=A.S. |last3=Dias |first3=L.S. |title=Responses of germination and early growth of scorzonera (Scorzonera hispanica L.) to pH, mineral deficiencies and growth substrates |journal=Bulgarian Journal of Agricultural Science |date=2014 |volume=20 |issue=5 |pages=1195–1201}}</ref><ref name="Bermejo, Neglected Crops">{{cite journal |last1=Hernándo Bermejo |first1=J.E. |last2=León |first2=J. |title=Neglected Crops: 1492 from a Different Perspective |journal=Plant Production and Protection Serie |date=1994 |issue=206 |pages=303–332}}</ref>

=== Harvesting and post-harvest treatment ===
[[Harvest]]ing takes place from November to March, with the optimum time for high quality being end of December.<ref name="Vulsteke" /> The process is somewhat complicated, as the roots are quite fragile, and broken material loses its freshness.<ref name="Hortipendium" /> Entire roots will keep fresh all winter if stored in a cool dark place, due to their robust black [[cork material|cork]]y skin. In [[root cellar]]s they may keep fresh well into springtime. The roots can also be washed, peeled, cut and then frozen.<ref name="Bermejo, Neglected Crops" /> In supermarkets, they can be bought conserved in glass or canned. On farmer’s markets, the roots are sold unwashed to secure quality and freshness.<ref name="Hortipendium" /> Black salsify is, however, very hardy and [[frost|frost-resistant]]<ref name="Nutzpflanzen">{{cite book |last1=Lieberei |first1=Reinhard |last2=Reisdorff |first2=Christoph |title=Nutzpflanzen |date=2012 |publisher=Thieme |location=Stuttgart |isbn=978-3-13-530408-3 |pages=271–272 |edition=8., überarb. Aufl}}</ref> and will grow well in most cool-[[temperate]] climates and usually yield 15–20 [[tonne]]s of roots per [[hectare]]. In British gardens it is common to profit from its perennial character by leaving it in the ground until its roots have grown to sufficient size for harvesting; this can take two years. Commercially, it can be grown best as the year's second crop. It is recommended to have three to four years in the [[crop rotation]] before the cultivation of other [[Asteraceae]].<ref name="Sativa">{{cite web |title=Schwarzwurzel |url=https://www.sativa-rheinau.ch/hausgarten/tipps/kulturblaetter/schwarzwurzel.html |website=Sativa Rheinau |publisher=Sativa Rheinau AG |access-date=9 November 2021}}</ref>

== Pests and diseases ==
=== Pests ===
* [[Carrot fly|Carrot rust fly]] (''Psila rosae''): The larvae or maggots of the carrot rust fly eat the plant roots and entrench themselves in the roots. ''Psila'' thereby inhibits plant growth and facilitates infection by soft-rot bacteria. Generally root crops are popular for the carrot rust fly.<ref name="rana_vcs" />
* Wireworms (''Selatosomus destructor and Ctenicera pruinina''): The wireworms are the larvae of [[click beetle]]s, which remain in the larval stage for between 2–5 years. They live in the soil and feed on roots. The wireworms cause a lot of damage when they bore directly into the roots. Plant pathogens can gain access through this, which can lead to rotting of the roots. Root rot can lead to wilting, stunting and deformation of the seedlings and eventually to death.<ref name="rana_vcs" />
* [[Root-knot nematode|Root knot nematode]] (''Meloidogyne incognita, M. javanica, M. hapla and M. arenaria''): Can cause great damage to the roots of salsify. Nematode activity damages growing root tips, causing branching, distortion, stunting and deformation of the taproot. The result can be general stunting, wilting and leaf chlorosis (yellowing) above ground.<ref name="rana_vcs" />

=== Diseases ===
* [[Bacterial soft rot]] (''Bacillus carotovorus'' Jones): The bacteria eat the root core. This can be recognised by a soft, watery and slimy root rot. This in turn facilitates infection by vertical fungi or bacteria. The ideal temperature for bacterial soft rot is 21 °C - 27 °C, but it can survive and cause damage at temperatures between 0 °C - 32 °C. For this reason, the air must be properly ventilated when storing and transporting the crop in tropical and warm environments.<ref name="rana_vcs" />
* White blister (''[[Albugo]]'' spp.): a leaf disease that favours wet weather. It is related to the pathogens of downy mildew and the two can also occur together. White blisters form blister-like white pustules on the underside of the leaves. A purple pigmentation is visible around the affected areas. This reduces plant growth and heavily infested plant parts may shrivel or even die.<ref name="rana_vcs" />
